Dermatology · published research

Radiation ulcers

Case reports and a three-case series describe complete closure after red-light laser treatment, usually within three to ten weeks. One report also measured increased dermal vessel counts. These favorable outcomes are uncontrolled, and several publications may describe overlapping patients.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Case reports and a three-case series describe complete closure after red-light laser treatment, usually within three to ten weeks. One report also measured increased dermal vessel counts. These favorable outcomes are uncontrolled, and several publications may describe overlapping patients.

Summary of the Evidence

Five publications are relevant to chronic radiation ulcers. Three are filed directly under radiation ulcers, one is a chronic-ulcer case report filed under radiation dermatitis, and one is a newer letter about radiation-related ulcers and fistulae. The four older Schindl publications came from the same research group; whether their patients overlap is unclear, and the three-case series may include earlier individual cases. The newer letter is indexed as a letter and has no abstract or accessible outcome details, so its patient-level results cannot be independently summarized here. No publication is a controlled comparison.

Human and clinical evidence

The 2000 case series reported complete closure in all three patients within five to eight weeks of low-intensity laser treatment. One patient died six weeks after treatment from cancer-related cachexia; the other two had no reported ulcer recurrence during 36 months of follow-up (Schindl et al. 2000). This is a direct, favorable wound outcome, although it is not a comparison against usual wound care.

Two 1997 case reports also described complete closure. One ulcer in a patient with lupus and diabetes healed 23 days after laser treatment began (Schindl et al. 1997). Another persistent radiation ulcer closed after 20 treatment sessions over ten weeks, with minimal scarring reported (Schindl et al. 1997). Because the same group published the later three-case series, these accounts should not automatically be counted as independent patients.

A related 1999 case, indexed under radiation dermatitis, described healing of a long-lasting radiation ulcer and a statistically significant increase in dermal vessel counts in both its central and marginal regions after treatment (Schindl et al. 1999). The article documents a measured tissue change alongside closure, but it does not establish that increased vessel count caused the healing.

A 2024 first-published letter, assigned to the broader radiation-induced-ulcer category, concerns chronic ulcerations and fistulae treated with PBM. The publisher identifies it as a letter and provides no abstract; the database record does not report enough case details or outcomes to add a specific closure estimate (Pünchera et al. 2025).

Animal evidence

No animal study directly addressing chronic radiation ulcers was identified in these records.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No indication-specific cell or ex-vivo study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The older case reports used 633-nm red visible helium-neon laser light. Reported fluences ranged from 30 to 36 J/cm², with schedules from seven sessions over four weeks to 20 sessions over ten weeks. The 2000 series used about 30 J/cm² three times weekly for five to eight weeks. The 1999 report specified 10 mW and 30 J/cm². Treatment was directed locally to the ulcer. Parameters for the newer letter are not available, and no study compared schedules or PBM with a control wound-care regimen.

Interpretation

Complete ulcer closure was reported repeatedly, and one case also showed increased dermal vessel counts. These outcomes make the human reports clinically relevant observations in difficult wounds. The effective number of independent patients is uncertain because the older publications may overlap, and the lack of controls means spontaneous change, wound care, and other factors cannot be separated from PBM. The reports support testing PBM in controlled radiation-wound studies, but do not establish comparative effectiveness or an optimal protocol.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for closure of chronic radiation ulcers with PBM
Publications and records5 articles (older case reports may overlap)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Several case reports and one small case series describe complete closure, and one report measured an increase in dermal vessel counts. These are favorable observations in difficult wounds, but the publications come largely from one group and may include overlapping patients. A prospective controlled study with defined wound care, dosimetry, closure criteria, and recurrence follow-up would support a stronger rating.
